narrative:
The 2020 Cincinnati Reds entered their coronavirus-shortened 60-game season with legitimate playoff aspirations, armed with a revamped rotation and key offseason additions like Mike Moustakas and Nick Castellanos. But the first week of play was a disaster, a brutal 2-5 July that saw the bullpen implode and the offense strand runners at the worst possible moments. Miguel Cabrera and JaCoby Jones torched Michael Lorenzen and Raisel Iglesias in back-to-back games against Detroit, and Joey Votto's clutch struggles in late-inning spots compounded the misery of a team that looked nothing like its billing.

August brought turbulence but also resilience. A Nick Castellanos error opened the floodgates against Detroit again early in the month, and a Christian Colón double play killed a rally against Kansas City, yet the Reds managed to go 13-15 — winning ugly and grinding out enough victories to stay in the Wild Card picture. The turning point came on August 21st, when journeyman Matt Davidson launched a grand slam that captured everything scrappy and unlikely about this Reds club, a moment of unlikely heroism that helped stabilize a roster still searching for its identity.

September was when Cincinnati finally looked like the team everyone expected. A 16-9 record in the final month validated the rotation's brilliance — Trevor Bauer was electric despite one rough outing against Pittsburgh — and the offense caught fire. Tyler Stephenson's two-run homer and Mike Moustakas's three-run blast on September 14th alone encapsulated a month full of clutch, high-leverage moments that pushed the Reds across the finish line and into the expanded postseason field for the first time since 2013.

The Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves, however, was a swift and painful reckoning. Played as a best-of-three, Cincinnati could never quite string enough together against a deep Atlanta roster. Jesse Winker and Eugenio Suárez provided flickers of hope, but Amir Garrett surrendered a Freddie Freeman single that brought the Reds to the brink, and Ronald Acuña's double the following day sealed their fate. The season ended as it had begun — with promise outpacing execution — leaving fans to wonder what might have been with a full 162 games and a little more fortune in October.

chapters.title: Opening Week Disasters
chapters.description: The Reds stumble out of the gate in a brutal 2-5 July, with the bullpen and offense both failing in critical moments.

chapters.title: Grinding Through August
chapters.description: Costly errors and double plays haunt Cincinnati early in the month, but Davidson's grand slam signals the team's fighting spirit.

chapters.title: September Surge
chapters.description: The Reds catch fire with a 16-9 record, as clutch home runs from Moustakas, Stephenson, and Suárez power Cincinnati into the postseason.

chapters.title: Wild Card Exit
chapters.description: Cincinnati's postseason run comes to a quick and painful end against the Atlanta Braves, with key stranded rallies and late-inning heartbreak ending the season.
